# Chapter 6 Practice: Thermochemistry

*Auto-generated from the assessment guide (`assessment-support/thermochemistry.md`), grouped by objective. 24 questions spanning multiple-choice, short-answer, and workout formats. Within each objective the questions run from easier to harder.*

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 1
{{sp[info] Objective 6.1a}} · *multiple-choice* A sealed glass flask sitting on a hot plate is best described as

A. an open system
B. a closed system
C. an isolated system
D. not a system at all
:::
::: tab Answer
**B.** It is sealed, so no matter crosses the boundary, but heat clearly does. An open system would exchange both; an isolated system neither.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 2
{{sp[info] Objective 6.1a}} · *short answer* An instant cold pack feels cold when you squeeze it. Is the dissolution inside it exothermic or endothermic? Explain how the sensation relates to the sign.
:::
::: tab Answer
**Endothermic.** The salt dissolving inside the pack *absorbs* heat from its surroundings.

Your hand is part of the surroundings, so your hand loses heat — which is what "feels cold" reports. The sensation always describes what happened to the surroundings, never to the system. Anything that feels cold is absorbing heat, and anything that feels hot is releasing it.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 3
{{sp[info] Objective 6.1a}} · *short answer* Classify each as a state function or not: temperature, heat, internal energy, work, enthalpy.
:::
::: tab Answer
**State functions:** temperature, internal energy, enthalpy. Each is fixed by the system's present condition, whatever route it took to get there.

**Not state functions:** heat and work. Both describe a *transfer* of energy, so their values depend entirely on the path taken between the two states.

This is exactly why Hess's Law works for $\Delta H$ but there is no corresponding law for $q$.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 4
{{sp[info] Objective 6.1b}} · *workout* A system absorbs 550 J of heat while 220 J of work is done on it. Find $\Delta U$.
:::
::: tab Answer
Sign both from the system's side. Heat absorbed: $q = +550$ J. Work done **on** the system: $w = +220$ J.

$$\Delta U = q + w = 550 + 220 = +770\ \text{J}$$

Both transfers added energy, so $\Delta U$ must be positive and larger than either alone.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 5
{{sp[info] Objective 6.1b}} · *workout* A gas releases 425 J of heat while expanding and doing 175 J of work on its surroundings. Find $\Delta U$.
:::
::: tab Answer
Both transfers now take energy *out* of the system, so both are negative: $q = -425$ J and $w = -175$ J.

$$\Delta U = -425 + (-175) = -600\ \text{J}$$

Contrast with Q4: the arithmetic is identical, and only the signs differ. Deciding the direction of each transfer before substituting is the whole method.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 6
{{sp[info] Objective 6.1b}} · *workout* A gas is compressed from 6.00 L to 2.00 L by a constant external pressure of 2.50 atm, releasing 890 J of heat in the process. Find $w$ and $\Delta U$ in joules. (1 L·atm = 101.3 J)
:::
::: tab Answer
**Work.** The gas is compressed, so $\Delta V$ is negative and $w$ comes out positive — work was done on the gas.

$$w = -P\Delta V = -(2.50\,\text{atm})(2.00 - 6.00\,\text{L}) = +10.0\ \text{L·atm}$$
$$10.0\,\text{L·atm}\times\frac{101.3\,\text{J}}{1\,\text{L·atm}} = +1013\ \text{J}$$

**First law.** Heat released means $q = -890$ J.

$$\Delta U = -890 + 1013 = +123\ \text{J}$$

The compression put in more energy than the heat loss removed, so the gas ends up with more internal energy despite cooling its surroundings.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 7
{{sp[info] Objective 6.2a}} · *multiple-choice* For an endothermic reaction,

A. $\Delta H < 0$ and the surroundings warm up
B. $\Delta H > 0$ and the surroundings cool down
C. $\Delta H > 0$ and the surroundings warm up
D. $\Delta H < 0$ and the surroundings cool down
:::
::: tab Answer
**B.** Endothermic means the system absorbs heat, so $\Delta H > 0$. That heat comes out of the surroundings, which therefore cool.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 8
{{sp[info] Objective 6.2a}} · *workout* Given $\ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l)}$, $\Delta H = -571.6$ kJ, find $\Delta H$ for (a) $\ce{H2O(l) -> H2(g) + \tfrac12 O2(g)}$ and (b) $\ce{4H2(g) + 2O2(g) -> 4H2O(l)}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
**(a)** The target is the original equation reversed *and* halved. Reversing flips the sign; halving halves the magnitude:
$$\Delta H = -\tfrac12(-571.6) = +285.8\ \text{kJ}$$

**(b)** The target is the original doubled, so $\Delta H$ doubles and the sign is unchanged:
$$\Delta H = 2(-571.6) = -1143.2\ \text{kJ}$$

Note that (a) needed two operations and (b) only one. Work out what was done to the equation before touching the number.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 9
{{sp[info] Objective 6.2a}} · *workout* For $\ce{CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(l)}$, $\Delta H = -890.5$ kJ. How much heat is released when 25.0 g of methane (16.04 g/mol) burns?
:::
::: tab Answer
The coefficient of $\ce{CH4}$ is 1, so the tabulated value is already per mole of methane.

$$25.0\,\text{g}\times\frac{1\,\text{mol}}{16.04\,\text{g}}\times\frac{-890.5\,\text{kJ}}{1\,\text{mol}} = -1388\ \text{kJ}$$

**About 1.39 × 10³ kJ is released.**
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 10
{{sp[info] Objective 6.2b}} · *workout* For $\ce{2NO(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$, $\Delta H = -114.1$ kJ. Find $\Delta U$ at 298 K.
:::
::: tab Answer
Count moles of **gas** only: 2 products against $2 + 1 = 3$ reactants, so $\Delta n = -1$.

$$\Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n RT = -114.1 - (-1)(8.314\times10^{-3})(298) = -111.6\ \text{kJ}$$

The gas volume shrank, so the atmosphere did work on the system and slightly less energy had to leave as heat.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 11
{{sp[info] Objective 6.2b}} · *short answer* For which of these is $\Delta H = \Delta U$? (a) $\ce{C(s) + O2(g) -> CO2(g)}$; (b) $\ce{2H2O2(l) -> 2H2O(l) + O2(g)}$; \(c) $\ce{AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) -> AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq)}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
The two are equal when $\Delta n = 0$, counting gas moles only.

**(a)** 1 mol gas produced, 1 mol consumed: $\Delta n = 0$. **Equal.** The carbon is a solid and does not count.

**(b)** 1 mol gas produced, none consumed: $\Delta n = +1$. **Not equal.**

**\(c)** No gases at all: $\Delta n = 0$. **Equal.**

Case (a) is the instructive one — gases appear on both sides but their total is unchanged, so no net expansion work is done.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 12
{{sp[info] Objective 6.3a}} · *workout* How much heat is needed to raise 500.0 g of water from 20.0 °C to 100.0 °C? ($s_\text{water} = 4.184$ J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹)
:::
::: tab Answer
$$q = ms\Delta T = (500.0)(4.184)(80.0) = 1.674\times10^5\ \text{J} = 167.4\ \text{kJ}$$
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 13
{{sp[info] Objective 6.3a}} · *workout* A 45.0 g piece of copper ($s = 0.385$ J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹) absorbs 875 J of heat. If it started at 25.0 °C, what is its final temperature?
:::
::: tab Answer
Rearrange $q = ms\Delta T$ for $\Delta T$:

$$\Delta T = \frac{q}{ms} = \frac{875\,\text{J}}{(45.0\,\text{g})(0.385\,\text{J g}^{-1}\,^\circ\text{C}^{-1})} = 50.5\ ^\circ\text{C}$$
$$T_\text{final} = 25.0 + 50.5 = 75.5\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

The same 875 J added to 45.0 g of *water* would raise it only 4.6 °C — copper's specific heat is about eleven times smaller, so it heats about eleven times as much.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 14
{{sp[info] Objective 6.3a}} · *workout* A 125 g block of aluminum ($s = 0.897$ J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹) at 185 °C is dropped into 300.0 g of water at 22.0 °C. What is the final temperature of both?
:::
::: tab Answer
Everything the aluminum loses, the water gains, and both end at the same final temperature $T$.

$$m_\text{Al}s_\text{Al}(T - 185) = -\,m_\text{w}s_\text{w}(T - 22.0)$$
$$(125)(0.897)(T - 185) = -(300.0)(4.184)(T - 22.0)$$
$$112.1(T - 185) = -1255.2(T - 22.0)$$
$$112.1T - 20{,}739 = -1255.2T + 27{,}614$$
$$1367.3T = 48{,}353 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T = 35.4\ ^\circ\text{C}$$

Sanity check: the answer must lie between 22.0 and 185 °C, and it does. It sits much closer to the water's starting temperature because the water both outweighs the aluminum and has a far larger specific heat.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 15
{{sp[info] Objective 6.3b}} · *short answer* Why does a bomb calorimeter measure $\Delta U$ while a coffee-cup calorimeter measures $\Delta H$?
:::
::: tab Answer
The bomb is **rigid and sealed**, so the volume cannot change. With $\Delta V = 0$, the expansion work $w = -P\Delta V$ is zero, so the first law reduces to $\Delta U = q$. Every joule appears as heat.

The coffee cup is **open to the atmosphere**, so the pressure is fixed at about 1 atm while the volume is free to change. That is precisely the condition under which the heat exchanged equals $\Delta H$ — which is why enthalpy was defined in the first place.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 16
{{sp[info] Objective 6.3b}} · *workout* Burning 1.50 g of a sample in a bomb calorimeter raises the temperature of 950 g of water from 21.6 °C to 26.9 °C. The bomb's heat capacity is 420 J/°C. Find $q_\text{rxn}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$\Delta T = 26.9 - 21.6 = 5.3\ ^\circ\text{C}$$
$$q_\text{water} = (950)(4.184)(5.3) = 21{,}066\ \text{J} \qquad q_\text{bomb} = (420)(5.3) = 2226\ \text{J}$$
$$q_\text{rxn} = -(21{,}066 + 2226) = -23{,}292\ \text{J} = -23.3\ \text{kJ}$$

The bomb is quoted as a heat capacity, so no mass appears in its term — the units tell you that.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 17
{{sp[info] Objective 6.3b}} · *workout* 100.0 mL of 0.500 M HCl and 100.0 mL of 0.500 M NaOH, both at 21.4 °C, are mixed in a coffee-cup calorimeter and reach 24.8 °C. Taking the mixture as water, find the heat released and $\Delta H$ per mole of water formed.
:::
::: tab Answer
**The heat.** Total volume 200.0 mL, so mass 200.0 g; $\Delta T = 3.4$ °C.

$$q_\text{solution} = (200.0)(4.184)(3.4) = 2845\ \text{J} = 2.85\ \text{kJ}$$

So $q_\text{rxn} = -2.85$ kJ.

**Per mole.** Each reactant supplies $0.1000\,\text{L}\times0.500\,\text{M} = 0.0500$ mol, so 0.0500 mol of water forms.

$$\Delta H = \frac{-2.85\ \text{kJ}}{0.0500\ \text{mol}} = -56.9\ \text{kJ/mol}$$

Close to the accepted −57.3 kJ/mol, and the same value you would get from any other strong acid with any other strong base — because the net ionic equation is always $\ce{H+ + OH- -> H2O}$.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 18
{{sp[info] Objective 6.4a}} · *short answer* State Hess's Law and explain what property of enthalpy makes it true.
:::
::: tab Answer
**Hess's Law:** the enthalpy change for a reaction is the same whether it happens in one step or in a series of steps. Equivalently, if a reaction can be written as the sum of other reactions, its $\Delta H$ is the sum of theirs.

It is true because **enthalpy is a state function** — its value depends only on the initial and final states, not on the route between them. If the route mattered, you could construct a cycle that created energy from nothing, which the first law forbids.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 19
{{sp[info] Objective 6.4a}} · *workout* Find $\Delta H^\circ$ for $\ce{2S(s) + 3O2(g) -> 2SO3(g)}$ from
$$\ce{S(s) + O2(g) -> SO2(g)}\qquad \Delta H_1^\circ = -296.8\ \text{kJ}$$
$$\ce{2SO2(g) + O2(g) -> 2SO3(g)}\qquad \Delta H_2^\circ = -197.8\ \text{kJ}$$
:::
::: tab Answer
The target needs **2** sulfur, so double equation 1; equation 2 already produces 2 $\ce{SO3}$, so use it as written.

$$2\Delta H_1^\circ = 2(-296.8) = -593.6\ \text{kJ}$$
$$\Delta H^\circ = -593.6 + (-197.8) = -791.4\ \text{kJ}$$

**Check that the intermediate cancels:** doubling equation 1 produces 2 $\ce{SO2}$, and equation 2 consumes 2 $\ce{SO2}$. ✓ And the oxygen: $2 + 1 = 3$ mol, matching the target. ✓
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 20
{{sp[info] Objective 6.4a}} · *workout* Find $\Delta H^\circ$ for $\ce{N2(g) + 2O2(g) -> 2NO2(g)}$ from
$$\ce{N2(g) + O2(g) -> 2NO(g)}\qquad \Delta H_1^\circ = +180.5\ \text{kJ}$$
$$\ce{2NO2(g) -> 2NO(g) + O2(g)}\qquad \Delta H_2^\circ = +114.1\ \text{kJ}$$
:::
::: tab Answer
$\ce{NO2}$ is a **product** in the target but a **reactant** in equation 2, so equation 2 must be **reversed** — which flips its sign.

$$-\Delta H_2^\circ = -114.1\ \text{kJ}$$
$$\Delta H^\circ = +180.5 + (-114.1) = +66.4\ \text{kJ}$$

**Check the intermediate cancels:** equation 1 produces 2 $\ce{NO}$ and the reversed equation 2 consumes 2 $\ce{NO}$. ✓ Oxygen: 1 mol from equation 1 plus 1 mol from the reversed equation 2 gives 2 mol, matching the target. ✓

Whenever a species appears on the wrong side, reversing is the move — and reversing always costs a sign.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 21
{{sp[info] Objective 6.4b}} · *short answer* Why is $\Delta H_\text{f}^\circ$ defined as zero for an element in its most stable form, and does that choice affect any calculated reaction enthalpy?
:::
::: tab Answer
Absolute enthalpies cannot be measured — only changes in enthalpy can. So a reference point has to be *chosen*, and elements in their standard states are the convenient choice because every compound can be built from them.

**It affects nothing.** Every reaction enthalpy is a difference between products and reactants, and any constant added to the reference level appears on both sides and cancels. Another zero would give the same reaction enthalpies with different tabulated numbers.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 22
{{sp[info] Objective 6.4b}} · *workout* Calculate $\Delta H_\text{rxn}^\circ$ for $\ce{2H2S(g) + 3O2(g) -> 2SO2(g) + 2H2O(l)}$, given $\Delta H_\text{f}^\circ$: $\ce{H2S(g)} = -20.6$, $\ce{SO2(g)} = -296.8$, $\ce{H2O(l)} = -285.8$ kJ/mol.
:::
::: tab Answer
Products minus reactants, each weighted by its coefficient. $\ce{O2(g)}$ is an element in its standard state, so it contributes zero.

$$\Delta H_\text{rxn}^\circ = [2(-296.8) + 2(-285.8)] - [2(-20.6) + 3(0)]$$
$$= (-1165.2) - (-41.2) = -1124.0\ \text{kJ}$$

Strongly exothermic, as a combustion should be.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 23
{{sp[info] Objective 6.4b}} · *workout* Using $\Delta H_\text{f}^\circ$: $\ce{NH3(g)} = -45.9$, $\ce{NO(g)} = +90.3$, $\ce{H2O(g)} = -241.8$ kJ/mol, find $\Delta H_\text{rxn}^\circ$ for $\ce{4NH3(g) + 5O2(g) -> 4NO(g) + 6H2O(g)}$.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$\Delta H_\text{rxn}^\circ = [4(+90.3) + 6(-241.8)] - [4(-45.9) + 5(0)]$$
$$= (361.2 - 1450.8) - (-183.6) = -1089.6 + 183.6 = -906.0\ \text{kJ}$$

Note that $\ce{NO}$ has a *positive* formation enthalpy — it is less stable than its elements — and the reaction is still strongly exothermic overall, because the water formed more than compensates. A single positive $\Delta H_\text{f}^\circ$ tells you nothing on its own about the reaction's direction.
:::
::::

:::: tabs
::: tab Q 24
{{sp[info] Objective 6.4b}} · *workout* Calculate $\Delta H_\text{rxn}^\circ$ for $\ce{C2H2(g) + \tfrac52 O2(g) -> 2CO2(g) + H2O(l)}$ using $\Delta H_\text{f}^\circ$: $\ce{C2H2(g)} = +227.4$, $\ce{CO2(g)} = -393.5$, $\ce{H2O(l)} = -285.8$ kJ/mol. Then say how much heat 1.00 g of acetylene (26.04 g/mol) releases.
:::
::: tab Answer
$$\Delta H_\text{rxn}^\circ = [2(-393.5) + (-285.8)] - [(+227.4) + \tfrac52(0)]$$
$$= (-1072.8) - (227.4) = -1300.2\ \text{kJ}$$

Per gram:
$$1.00\,\text{g}\times\frac{1\,\text{mol}}{26.04\,\text{g}}\times\frac{-1300.2\,\text{kJ}}{1\,\text{mol}} = -49.9\ \text{kJ}$$

Acetylene's positive formation enthalpy is doing real work here: because the compound starts *above* its elements, tearing it apart releases energy rather than costing it, and that extra 227 kJ/mol is added to the combustion. This is why an oxyacetylene torch burns hot enough to cut steel.
:::
::::
